Keep the response about 500 words. # steering-lite steering-lite changes a model's hidden activations during inference, without retraining. When we steer a model, we want to change one thing without changing everything else. We might want less sycophancy, for example, while keeping its answers to ordinary factual questions the same. Give it pairs of prompts showing opposite behaviours, extract a steering vector, and apply it while the model generates. How well that works depends on the method and the strength of the steer. The code is meant to be easy to change: one file per method, starting with [mean_diff.py](src/steering_lite/variants/mean_diff.py). It is a sister project of [lora-lite](https://github.com/wassname/lora-lite), for activation steering rather than adapter fine-tuning. [Results](#results) · [Try it](#quickstart) · [Add a method](#add-a-method) · [Value maps](https://github.com/wassname/moral-maps#can-we-steer-these-values) ## Results We steer Qwen3.5-9B on the 100 [BullshitBench v2](https://github.com/petergpt/bullshit-benchmark) questions, which all contain a nonsense premise. +C steers toward going along with the nonsense, −C toward pushing back. Each method gets 3 seeds and a sweep from weak to strong.
Figure 1: Steering Qwen3.5-9B on BullshitBench v2: each line is one method swept from weak to strong. Left is pushing back on the nonsense, right is going along with it; lower means more else changed.
The gray shows how much random interventions can change model sycophancy (horizontal) vs side effects (vertical). The sweeps show that as we increase the dose of a steering intervention, it gets stronger effects and side effects, until it breaks down. I compare to prompting, which I suspect is better if the model wants to change behaviour as instructed, and worse if it doesn't.

One row per method. Each side uses the method's best dose: the largest premise change minus other change, with other change at most 1.5 in every seed. A judge model (Jev) compares each steered answer with the unsteered one and rates the change in premise acceptance (−3..+3) and how much everything else changed (0..4). The score is premise change minus other change, on the weaker side. −C pushback is reduced by 3 × the rise in legitimate control questions called nonsense (unsteered: 3%); random has no control questions. — means no dose passed in every seed. [more columns](slop/reviews/2026-10-07_cache_mean_diff/table.md) · [setup details](slop/specs/20261006_bsbench_eval_frozen.md) · [earlier evaluations](slop/research/20261007_historical_bsbench_results/README.md) The score has a weak spot. A method can score well by barely changing anything: `cache_mean_diff` is near the top for this reason, not because it steers well. I hope we can use this to show how good steering methods are, and make better ones. ## Quickstart From a local checkout, install with `uv pip install -e ".[hf-test]"`. The example uses a CUDA GPU. ``` python import torch import steering_lite as sl from steering_lite import Vector from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ).cuda() tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B") pos = ["I want to be helpful and honest.", "I will tell the truth."] neg = ["I will deceive you.", "I will lie to you."] v = Vector.train(model, tok, pos, neg, sl.MeanDiffC()).calibrate(model, tok) inputs = tok("Tell me about yourself.", return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) with v(model): out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64) print(tok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)) v.save("honesty.safetensors") v2 = Vector.load("honesty.safetensors") ``` This shows the API; two prompt pairs are not an evaluation of honesty. Vectors can be scaled with `v * 0.5`, and compatible vectors can be added with `v + v2`. ## How strongly should we steer? How do we compare methods when one might be strong and one weak? These are calibration questions. We measure how much steering changes the next-token distribution using KL divergence. Calibration finds a coefficient that reaches the requested divergence budget on a set of prompts, then stores it in the vector. The default `Vector.calibrate` target is 1 nat using the root-mean-square token KL over short, 50-token rollouts. This makes intervention strength more comparable; it does not guarantee that the model remains useful. ``` python v.calibrate(model, tok, target_kl=1.0, target_stat="kl_rms") ``` ## Add a method Write one file in [the variants directory](src/steering_lite/variants), register it, and add its name to `METHODS` in `tests/test_pipeline.py`. Then test it in three steps: ``` bash just check # tiny random models on CPU: catches crashes, scores mean nothing just dev my_method # Qwen3.5-9B, 1 seed, 20 questions, compared with every finished method just sweep my_method # the full run: 3 seeds, 100 questions; then `just pull` and `just results` ``` `just dev` and `just sweep` need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), [just](https://github.com/casey/just), pnpm, a Modal account and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `.env`. They cost GPU time and judge credits. Finished answers and ratings are cached and reused. ## Methods Each file includes its math and paper references. Start with [mean difference](src/steering_lite/variants/mean_diff.py) or [PCA](src/steering_lite/variants/pca.py). Newer variants are [VJP residual](src/steering_lite/variants/vjp_resid.py), [VJP value](src/steering_lite/variants/vjp_value.py), [Value Gram](src/steering_lite/variants/value_gram.py), [query steering](src/steering_lite/variants/query_steer.py) and [cache mean difference](src/steering_lite/variants/cache_mean_diff.py). [Random](src/steering_lite/variants/random.py) is the null baseline. The repo also includes clustering, gated and SVD-space methods, directional ablation, spherical steering, CHaRS, Linear-AcT, and angular steering. See also [weight-steering](https://github.com/wassname/weight-steering), [IBM AISteer360](https://github.com/IBM/AISteer360), and [repeng](https://github.com/vgel/repeng). ## Citation ``` bibtex @misc{wassname2026steeringlite, title = {steering-lite}, author = {Michael J Clark}, year = {2026}, url = {https://github.com/wassname/steering-lite} } ```

, here is an assessment of the steering-lite library, its benchmarks, and related details:

### 1. What the Library Does and Benchmark Measurements

**What the Library Does:**
The `steering-lite` library is designed to modify the behavior of pre-trained language models during text generation *without the

need for retraining*. It achieves this by altering the model's internal "hidden activations." The core idea is to provide pairs of prompts that demonstrate opposite behaviors (e.g., one encouraging sycophancy, another discouraging it). The library then extracts a "steering vector" from these examples and applies it during the model's inference process

. The goal is to change a specific aspect of the model's output, such as reducing sycophancy, while attempting to keep its general capabilities, like answering factual questions, intact. It is positioned as a counterpart to methods like LoRA, focusing on activation steering rather than adapter fine-tuning.

**

What the Benchmark Measures:**
The benchmark assesses different steering methods by applying them to the Qwen3.5-9B model using the 100 questions from the BullshitBench v2 dataset. These questions are characterized by containing a nonsensical premise. The benchmark measures how well each method steers the model's response, specifically

concerning its acceptance of the nonsense premise and the degree to which other parts of the generated answer are affected (referred to as "side effects"). Each method is tested across a range of "strengths" (from weak to strong steering) and across multiple random seeds. The performance is evaluated using a judge model that rates premise

acceptance changes and "other change" in the output.

**Meaning of +C and −C:**
In the context of this benchmark, "+C" signifies steering *towards* going along with or accepting the nonsense premise presented in the question. Conversely, "−C" signifies steering *towards* pushing back against

or rejecting the nonsense premise.

### 2. What the Plot Shows

The plot (Figure 1) visualizes the performance of various steering methods on the Qwen3.5-9B model and BullshitBench v2.
*   **X-axis:** Represents the "change in premise acceptance

" compared to the unsteered model. Moving to the **right** means the model is more likely to go along with the nonsense premise, while moving to the **left** means it pushes back against it.
*   **Y-axis:** Represents "how much else in the answer changed" (side effects).

A value of **0** at the top indicates minimal other changes, while increasing values downwards (up to 1.6 shown) indicate more significant alterations to the rest of the model's output.
*   **Lines:** Each colored line corresponds to a specific steering method. These lines show how the method's performance (premise

acceptance vs. other change) evolves as the steering strength is swept from weak (near the top, less change) to strong (further down). Most methods reach a premise acceptance of about +1.8 on the right before significant "other change" occurs. On the left (pushback), only the "VJP-resid" method achieves

substantial pushback (around -1.0) within a reasonable "other change" margin.
*   **Grey Area:** The grey bands illustrate the effect of 20 random directions for intervention, showing the typical range of premise acceptance and side effects achievable by random steering.
*   **Stars:** The stars

represent results obtained by "prompting" (likely through specific prompt engineering). They show a modest increase in premise acceptance (+0.5) on the right, but on the left, the pushback is negated because prompting also incorrectly labels legitimate questions as nonsense.

### 3. Table Row Interpretation and Best Method

**

Meaning of a Table Row:**
Each row in Table 1 represents a single steering method's performance on the Qwen3.5-9B model using the BullshitBench v2. The values shown are derived from the "best dose" for each method, which is defined as the largest premise change achieved

minus the corresponding "other change," with the constraint that "other change" does not exceed 1.5.
*   `method`: The name of the steering technique.
*   `score↑`: An overall performance metric, calculated as premise change minus other change, particularly emphasizing performance on the "weaker side

" (though the text doesn't explicitly define "weaker side" in this context). The arrow indicates higher is better.
*   `−C pushback↑`: The amount of premise acceptance change when steering *away* from the nonsense. Higher is better.
*   `−C other↓`:

The amount of unrelated changes in the output when steering *away* from the nonsense. Lower is better.
*   `+C goes along↑`: The amount of premise acceptance change when steering *towards* accepting the nonsense. Higher is better.
*   `+C other↓`: The amount of unrelated changes

in the output when steering *towards* accepting the nonsense. Lower is better.
*   `legit rejected↓`: The percentage of legitimate questions (presumably those without a nonsense premise) that were incorrectly flagged as nonsense by the steered model. Lower is better.

**Which Method Does Best and How to Know:**

The document does not explicitly state which method is "best" overall without ambiguity. However, it provides several ways to interpret performance:
*   **Highest `score↑`:** The `vjp_resid` method has the highest score at **-0.03**.
*   **Highest `+C goes

along↑`:** The `topk_clusters` method achieved the highest value of **+1.95**.
*   **Highest `−C pushback↑`:** The `vjp_resid` method also achieved the highest pushback at **+1.00**.
*   **Lowest

side effects (`−C other↓`, `+C other↓`):** Several methods show low "other" changes, often around 0.20-0.29, with `cache_mean_diff` and `vjp_value` being examples.
*   **Lowest `legit rejected↓`:** Most

methods have a low rejection rate (around 3%), but `vjp_resid` is higher (12%), and `prompting` is significantly higher (48%).

The text states that `vjp_resid` has the highest `score↑`. However, it also notes that the score "has a weak spot.

A method can score well by barely changing anything: `cache_mean_diff` is near the top for this reason, not because it steers well." This suggests that the `score` alone might be misleading and that other metrics like the magnitude of premise change (`+C` or `-C` values) are also

important.

**Meaning of "−C other" and "legit rejected":**
*   `−C other`: This refers to the degree of unintended changes in the model's output when the steering is applied to push back against a nonsensical premise. A lower number indicates fewer side effects.
*   `

legit rejected`: This is the percentage of standard, legitimate questions (not containing nonsense) that the steered model incorrectly identified as nonsense. A lower percentage signifies that the steering method does not degrade the model's ability to handle normal queries.

### 4. Why a High Score Might Not Indicate Good Steering

A method might

achieve a high score but not actually steer well because the scoring metric (premise change minus other change) can be gamed. If a method produces a large premise change but *very little* "other change," its score will be high. However, the text explicitly states, "A method can score well by barely changing anything:

`cache_mean_diff` is near the top for this reason, not because it steers well." This implies that a high score doesn't necessarily mean the steering is *effective* at making the desired change in a meaningful way, but rather that it has achieved a good *ratio* of desired change to side effects

, potentially by making only minimal progress on the desired change.

### 5. Testing a New Method

**What to Run:**
If you wanted to test a new method, you would first write the method's logic in a Python file within the `src/steering_lite/variants/` directory. Then, you

would register it and add its name to the `METHODS` list in `tests/test_pipeline.py`. After setting up necessary tools like `uv`, `just`, pnpm, a Modal account, and an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, you would run the following commands:
1.  `

just check`: This command runs a quick test on tiny random models on a CPU. It primarily catches immediate crashes and is not meant for meaningful performance evaluation.
2.  `just dev my_method`: This command performs a development test for your new method (replace `my_method` with its name). It runs on

Qwen3.5-9B, uses 1 seed and 20 questions, and compares your method against all already finished methods.
3.  `just sweep my_method`: This is the full testing procedure. It runs your method with 3 seeds and 100 questions. After this

completes, you would run `just pull` to fetch results and then `just results` to generate the final performance tables and plots.

**What Each Command Tells You:**
*   `just check`: Tells you if your method code is syntactically correct and doesn't immediately crash the basic pipeline.
*   `just

dev my_method`: Gives a preliminary indication of your method's performance relative to established ones on a smaller scale, identifying major issues or promising behavior early. It helps catch bugs or significant performance disparities before a full sweep.
*   `just sweep my_method`: This is the comprehensive evaluation. It measures your

method's effectiveness across multiple random variations (seeds) and a full dataset, providing robust performance metrics comparable to all other methods listed in the results. It generates the data needed for the plots and tables.
